newsitem.title: INDIA: Low metal prices hit India Hindalco net.
newsitem.headline: Low metal prices hit India Hindalco net.

text.p: Low global aluminium prices and a power shortage due to a grid failure lowered the net of leading private aluminium maker Hindalco Industries in the financial year ended March 31, 1997, analysts said.
Hindalco said its 1996/97 (April-March) net profit slipped to 3.91 billion rupees, from 4.01 billion rupees. Net sales fell to 11.57 billion rupees from 12.52 billion in 1995/96.

"Given the industry scenario, the tremendous dip in the London Metal Exchange (LME) prices, the breakdown in the state grid resulting in disruption of power supply... Hindalco has reported truly encouraging results," the firm said.
Global aluminium prices fell sharply on the LME to $1,286 a tonne last October from $2,146 a tonne in January 1995, before reversing a prolonged downtrend.
LME prices are currently trading at around $1,550 a tonne.
Hindalco said a power disturbance caused by a grid failure in April 1996 hit production during the year, pulling metal output down to 166,272 tonnes, from 175,398 tonnes in 1995/96.
Output of rolled products dropped sharply to 18,302 tonnes from 31,378, but Hindalco said the outlook remained bright.

"Higher volumes, a larger share for value-added products, improved cost efficiency, strengthening international prices and increased aluminium production will fuel the company's growth to new heights," the company said in a statement.
Hindalco plans to expand its alumina refinery capacity to 450,000 tonnes a year from the current 350,000 tonnes. The project is due to be commissioned by during 1997/98.
Analysts said the results were in line with expectations, and most said they were maintaining their "buy" recommendation on the stock.
"There were no surprises," said analyst Chetan Ahya at Caspian Securities. "The company is going to see a 20 percent volume growth next year and we have a buy on the stock."
He forecast an earnings growth of more than 45 percent in 1997/98 and said his projections were based on an average LME price of a "conservative" $1,650 during the year.
Analysts said domestic imports had risen sharply towards the end of calendar 1996, as downstream users took advantage of the lower prices resulting in a glut.
"Global prices were very low and downstream users contracted a lot of material which entered the market in October-November," said an analyst at HSBC Batlivala & Karani Securities.
"Imports for the industry shot up forcing aluminium makers to offer discounts ranging from six to 10 percent," he said.
As a result, exports of aluminium makers like Hindalco and NALCO increased during 1996/97.
Hindalco's exports jumped to 1.57 billion rupees, from 1.05 billion in the previous year.
"Export realisations are lower and that also affected operating margins," the HSBC analyst said.
